name: Jehai
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 further works by the same author (or citing it for stress) agree. 2 further first-hand descriptions conflict (see the conflicting-description items); the entry follows Burenhult 2005.

tone_statements.citation: Hajek, John. 2003. Evidence of tonal activity in Aslian. Mon-Khmer Studies 33: 59-66.
tone_statements.quote: As long ago as the 1920s, Schebesta (1926:205) reported a simple two way (high v. low) tone contrast in a small set of monosyllables in Jahai, given at (1) [...] More recently, however, Burenhult (2001) found no such evidence in the variety of Jahai he was able to record and describe. [...] The difference between his and Burenhult's finding suggest instead that tone where it occurs in Jahai is either not characteristic of all varieties of Jahai, or that the rare examples of contrastive tone first reported by Schebesta (1926) may have been lost in Jahai in the intervening seventy years. (pp. 59-60)

tone_statements.summary: Nothing on stress. Second-hand: six Schebesta (1926) high/low monosyllable pairs (e.g. jor 'part of a blowpipe' v. jor 'bough', nus 'sleeping mat' v. nus 'lip') set against Burenhult (2001) finding no tone. The catalog's Jahai tone field is empty; this supplies a marginal-tone note (possibly variety-specific or lost), not a system change.

tone_statements.summary: The catalog classes Jahai as no-tone (Burenhult 2005). Schebesta 1928 reports, with an explicit hedge ('I believe I have detected'), a high-level vs low-level tone contrast in six lexical pairs, marked in the text with raised and lowered bar diacritics. A 1928 impressionistic claim, not an instrumental one; it disagrees with the catalog's tone class but does not touch the stress rule.

audit.deciding_source_kind: database or survey citing another work
audit.reasoning: Coding 'fixed-dominant, final (final stress)' is correct and now verified against the primary reference grammar: Burenhult 2005 sec. 2.5.1 p.38 states non-contrastive stress invariably on the last syllable of the word, no secondary stress, applying equally to Malay loans (sec. 2.6.4 p.43 gives /ga'jah/ < Malay 'gajah as relocation to final); Burenhult 2001 MKS 31 p.43 is identical; Wikipedia's sentence is a faithful paraphrase. The record as filed rests on Wikipedia with grade carried-secondary only because the compilers could not reach the primary; the primary is now obtained (sealang PL-566 PDF with text). sources.citation: Wikipedia, Jahai language, Stress and tone section (citing Burenhult 2005 A Grammar of Jahai); corroborates the verification Burenhult p.38 quote (invariable final stress, no secondary stress, applies to loans).
sources.quote: The position of stress always falls on the last syllable.

sources.citation: Burenhult, Niclas. 2005. A Grammar of Jahai. Pacific Linguistics 566. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, ANU. xiv+245 pp.
sources.quote: 'As also noted by Schebesta (1928a:805), Jahai has non-contrastive stress that falls invariably on the last syllable of a word, and there is no secondary stress. This applies as much to recent loans from Malay as to indigenous words.' Elsewhere: unstressed preverbal pronouns/clitics 'cannot receive stress'; reduplicant copies do not receive stress.
sources.locator: sec. 2.5.1 'Stress', p.38 (p.52); also sec. 2.4.2 (final syllable 'always bears stress') and sec. 2.6.4 p.43 'Relocation of stress' (Malay loans get final stress: /ga'jah/ < 'gajah)

sources.locator: p. 805, section 'Stress and Tone'; also p. 804, translator's introductory note signed C; O; B.: 'The syllabic stress being on the final syllable tends to reduc…
sources.note: Confirms the Jahai catalog rule (fixed final stress, Burenhult 2005). Domain stated as 'a word'. No secondary stress mentioned (catalog: stated none). No weight condition; long vowels exist (la:b, te:g, babo:) and 'in rapid connected speech long vowels are sometimes shortened' (p. 804) but length is not tied to stress. No exceptions stated. Impressionistic field description, no instruments.

sources.citation: Burenhult, Niclas (2003). Attention, accessibility, and the addressee: The case of the Jahai demonstrative ton. Pragmatics 13. pp. 363-379.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.locator: p. 367, section 1.3 'The characteristics of Jahai ton'
sources.note: The paper is a pragmatic study of the nominal demonstrative ton (attentional/accessibility semantics), based on ~90 min of video-recorded Shape Classifier Task interaction with three native male speakers (p. 369). Its only prosodic remark is that the demonstrative ton is 'rarely stressed' in discourse (p. 367), a statement about phrasal/sentential prominence of one function word, not a description of the word-stress system.
